html:
A trading quarter outside the city of Kanesh, near Kayseri in central Anatolia, where merchants from Assur lived and worked from about 1950 to 1750 BCE. The Assyrians called such a quarter a karum, "quay".

Donkey caravans brought tin and woollen cloth some 1,000 kilometres from Assur to Anatolia. The tin came from further east; much of the cloth was made in Babylonia. The merchants sold the goods for silver and gold, which went back home. Firms were often run by families, with partners in both cities, and investors pooled money for long ventures.

Over 23,000 clay tablets have been found in the merchants' houses: letters, contracts, loans and court cases written in Old Assyrian cuneiform. They form the oldest large business archive in the world. Local names in them give the earliest record of an Indo-European language, the tongue later written by the Hittite kingdom, whose people called it Nesite after Nesa, another name for Kanesh. The trade shows Assyria as a merchant city long before it was an empire.
